title: Tax Credits People Commonly Miss
summary: TOTAL THE HOUSEHOLD → CHECK THE DTC → FILE PROVINCIAL TOO
subtitle: If nobody mailed you a slip, your software will not ask about it. Most of the real money is unclaimed for that reason alone.

blocks.text: Tax software is excellent at one thing: taking every T4, T5 and RRSP slip you upload and putting the numbers in the right boxes. It is much less good at knowing that you drove your father to dialysis fourteen times last year, or that a doctor told you to put in a stair lift.
None of that arrives on a slip. All of it can be worth real money on your return.
What this course does
Almost everything here follows the same pattern. No paper shows up in the mail to remind you, so the credit only gets claimed by people who already knew to look for it. This module is the looking.
Claiming the credits no slip reminds you about can put real money back in your household.
blocks.detail: Medical costs, caregiving and a family member’s disability status are worth money only if someone enters them.
blocks.extra: Section 02 shows how wide the medical credit reaches.

sections.title: Medical expenses: wider than almost anyone assumes

blocks.text: Most people claim the obvious: prescriptions, dental work and glasses. The credit reaches much further, and it covers your household. You can claim costs for yourself, your spouse and the people who depend on you, including adult children, parents and grandparents. In some cases you can also claim for brothers, sisters, aunts, uncles, nieces and nephews who rely on you.

People often miss two things. First, travel. If you had to go at least 40 kilometres one way for medical care you could not get near home, you can claim the travel. Past 80 kilometres, you can add meals and a place to stay. Second, items beyond prescriptions. These include braces, hearing aids, wigs after a medical condition, air conditioners a doctor recommends, and home changes for someone who has trouble moving around. Several of those also connect to the Home Accessibility Tax Credit in the Senior Home-Renovation Programs lesson.

The claim has a floor. You can only claim the part above a set amount that changes each year, or above three percent of net income, whichever is lower. That floor is exactly why it matters whose return carries the claim.

items.title: “Everyone should claim their own medical expenses on their own return.”
items.text: The claim can go on either spouse’s return. Putting it on the lower-income spouse’s return often clears the floor with fewer receipts and gives a bigger credit. Add up every household member’s costs, then decide together whose return carries them. Do not just default to whoever paid.

sections.title: The Canada Caregiver Credit: for people who never call themselves a caregiver

blocks.text: This credit is for anyone supporting a spouse, partner or dependant with a physical or mental impairment. Many people giving exactly that support do not think of themselves as caregivers. They think of themselves as someone whose mother lives with them, or whose adult son will always need some support. The CRA’s meaning is broader than the word feels.

It also stacks with other help. A dependant who qualifies for this credit often qualifies for the Disability Tax Credit too. That, in turn, can open the Home Accessibility Tax Credit, a Registered Disability Savings Plan and a larger amount under this same credit. One form, filled in once by a medical practitioner, can be the key to several benefits. It is the same door-opener pattern from the Veteran Benefits lesson, turning up again.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE FORM THAT UNLOCKS THE MOST, AND GETS FILED THE LEAST

The Disability Tax Credit is the most useful single form in this whole module. A medical practitioner fills in form T2201 to set it up. It is a credit on its own, and it is also the key to the higher caregiver amount, the Home Accessibility Tax Credit at any age, the Registered Disability Savings Plan and its matching grants, and several provincial programs. It can also be backdated. If a practitioner confirms the condition existed in past years, the CRA can adjust up to ten years of old returns. Now and then, that produces a refund big enough to pay for a renovation, clear a debt or arrive as a pleasant surprise. It is also often turned down on a thin first try and approved on a second try with clearer medical detail about how the condition limits daily life. A no is feedback on the paperwork, not a final verdict on the person.

sections.title: Working and raising a family: the quiet ones

items.title: Child care expenses
list: Not only daycare. Camps, before-and-after-school programs and caregivers all qualify.
The receipt needs the provider’s SIN or business number, a detail that trips people up every spring.

items.title: Moving expenses
list: If you moved at least 40 kilometres closer to a new job, business or full-time study program, a long list of costs is deductible.
Movers, travel, temporary lodging, and the costs of selling the old home and buying the new one.

items.title: Tuition transfer
list: A student who cannot use all their tuition credit this year can transfer up to a set amount to a spouse, parent or grandparent.
Families routinely default to carry-forward without comparing which choice is worth more right now.

items.title: Home office expenses
list: For employees required to work from home, a share of costs like utilities, internet and rent is claimable with the right employer-signed form.
The pandemic-era flat rate is gone. The current process rewards keeping records through the year, not assembling them in April.

items.title: Canada Training Credit and Canada Workers Benefit
list: Covered in the Training Grants lesson, and worth a second mention here.
Both are refundable, both are easy to miss because neither arrives with a slip, and both are worth checking every year regardless of what you claimed last.

items.title: “Tax software catches everything I am entitled to automatically.”
items.text: Software is built to process what you enter, and it handles slips well. Anything without a slip, like caregiving, medical travel, a family member’s disability status or a move mid-year, has to be entered by you. The software has no way to know it happened.

sections.title: Refundable versus non-refundable, one more time

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: REFUNDABLE VERSUS NON-REFUNDABLE, ONE MORE TIME

This difference runs through the whole Platinum level for a reason. It is the one fact most likely to decide whether a credit is worth chasing at all. A non-refundable credit only lowers tax you owe. If your income is low enough that your tax bill is already near zero, more non-refundable credits do not put money in your pocket. A refundable credit is paid to you either way. That is why the Canada Training Credit, the Canada Workers Benefit and several provincial credits for caregivers matter so much for households with lower incomes. Before you decide a credit is not worth the paperwork for someone on a fixed or modest income, check which kind it is. The paperwork is often the same. The payoff is not.

sections.title: Do not stop at the federal return

blocks.text: Every province and territory runs its own credits alongside the federal ones: caregiver amounts, disability top-ups, home renovation credits like the ones in the Senior Home-Renovation Programs lesson, tax cuts for low incomes, and climate or carbon rebates. They run on a separate schedule from the federal return. They get less attention, because none of them has a single national name, and they are just as easy to miss. Check your province’s tax credit page once a year, the same way you check the federal one.

items.title: Medical expenses for every household member, not just yourself, totalled before deciding whose return carries the claim.
Whether anyone in the household might qualify for the Disability Tax Credit and has never applied.
Caregiving support you provide but have never labelled as caregiving.
A move, a new job, or a return to school in the past year that might unlock a deduction.
Whether last year’s return should be adjusted. The CRA generally allows amendments going back several years.
Your province’s own credits, checked separately from the federal list.

sections.title: Priyanka, her mother, and the form that had been sitting there for years

blocks.text: Priyanka and her mother
paragraphs: Priyanka’s mother moved in with her three years ago, after a stroke left her unable to get around easily. Priyanka drives her to two specialist visits a month and manages her pills. She has never once called herself a caregiver. It is just what a daughter does.

Her goal this year is simple: catch up on bills after paying for a wheelchair ramp. At her yearly meeting with her accountant, he asks a question nobody has asked before. Has your mother’s doctor ever filled in a Disability Tax Credit form?
Priyanka says no. It never crossed her mind that a stroke this serious might not count as a disability on paper unless someone applies.
She almost lets it go. The doctor is busy, and the form sounds like one more thing on a full plate. Then she decides to book the appointment anyway.
The form takes one visit. The approval covers this year. Then her accountant asks one more question, and the CRA backdates the credit three more years, to the month of the stroke.

The twist is how far it reaches. Three old returns are adjusted, her caregiver credit grows from now on, and her mother now qualifies for programs Priyanka had never looked at. The ramp is mostly paid for by spring.
Nothing about her mother’s health changed. The only thing that changed was a form being filled in by someone who finally thought to ask.

blocks.text: The credits that go unclaimed are the ones with no slip: medical travel, caregiving, a family member’s disability with no paperwork, a move mid-year. Add up your household’s medical costs before you decide whose return carries them. Ask whether anyone should have a Disability Tax Credit form on file. Check your province’s credits separately from the federal ones. None of it arrives by mail. All of it has to be asked for.
Priyanka’s family got three years of adjustments and a bigger caregiver credit from one form she almost skipped.
blocks.detail: Asking whether anyone in your home should have a Disability Tax Credit form can unlock the same chain of help.
blocks.extra: Your action this week, in Section 08, starts with your household’s medical costs.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Missed-Credit Check

items.title: List every medical expense across your household for this year, including travel, and note who paid and whose return might carry the claim.
Ask directly: does anyone in my household have a condition that might qualify for the Disability Tax Credit and has never applied? If yes, book the appointment to have the form completed.
Check your province’s tax credit page for anything that has no federal equivalent.

blocks.text: Worksheet: your missed-credit check
One rule of thumb: if your honest answer to a question below is “we never thought about it,” that is the exact answer this form is built to catch.

items.title: DTC
items.text: Disability Tax Credit. Proof of a severe, long-term condition, set up with form T2201. It opens the door to several other credits.

items.title: Canada Caregiver Credit
items.text: For a spouse, partner or dependant with a physical or mental condition who relies on you for support.

items.title: Refundable vs non-refundable
items.text: A refundable credit is paid to you whether or not you owe tax. A non-refundable credit only lowers tax you owe.

items.title: T2201
items.text: The Disability Tax Credit Certificate, filled in by a medical practitioner.

items.title: Notice of Reassessment
items.text: The CRA’s reply to a request to change a past return, such as a backdated disability credit.

items.title: Net income threshold (medical expenses)
items.text: The floor below which medical costs cannot be claimed: a set dollar amount that changes each year, or 3% of net income, whichever is lower.

items.title: WHERE TO GET HELP
list: Canada Revenue Agency: 1-800-959-8281, for questions about any credit in this module.
Community Volunteer Income Tax Program: free tax preparation and filing help for modest-income households, including prior-year adjustment requests.
A tax professional or accountant: for household-level decisions, like whose return should carry a shared medical claim.

blocks.text: This module skips dollar amounts on purpose. Thresholds, credit rates and provincial amounts are indexed and revised regularly. Confirm current figures on canada.ca and your provincial tax credit page before filing.

quiz.question: True or False: “Everyone should claim their own medical expenses on their own return.”

questions: Who in your household had medical costs this year, and about how much for each person? Estimates are fine.
Did anyone travel 40 kilometres or more, one way, for medical care? (Yes / No / Not sure)
Does anyone in your home have a long-term condition that limits daily life and has never applied for the Disability Tax Credit? (Yes / No / Not sure)
Do you help support a family member who lives with you or depends on you? Describe it in a few words.
Did you move for work or school, start a job or go back to school this year? Write “no changes” if not.
Have you checked your province’s own tax credits this year? (Yes / Not yet / Not sure)
